chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Verona. An open place
paragraphs: [Valentine and Proteus enter.]

VALENTINE. Stop trying to persuade me, my dear Proteus. Young men who stay at home always have small-town minds. If love didn’t chain your young days to the sweet looks of the woman you adore, I’d rather beg you to come with me and see the wonders of the world abroad. That beats living dully at home like a sluggard, wasting your youth in idleness with no shape to it. But since you’re in love, keep loving, and may it go well for you, just as I’d want it to go for me when I start loving.

PROTEUS. Are you really going? Sweet Valentine, goodbye. Think of your Proteus when you happen to see some rare, remarkable thing on your travels. Wish that I were there to share your happiness when good luck finds you. And when you’re in danger, if danger ever surrounds you, hand your troubles over to my holy prayers. I’ll be the one who prays for you, Valentine.
VALENTINE. And you’ll pray for my success on a book of love stories?
PROTEUS. I’ll pray for you on some book I love.
VALENTINE. That means on some shallow story about deep love, like how young Leander swam across the Hellespont.
PROTEUS. That’s a deep story about an even deeper love, because he was in love deeper than over his shoes.
VALENTINE. That’s true, because you’re in love up over your boots, and yet you never swam the Hellespont.
PROTEUS. Over my boots? No, don’t make fun of me with that boot joke.
VALENTINE. No, I won’t, because it does you no good.
PROTEUS. What doesn’t?

VALENTINE. Being in love, where you buy scorn with groans and cold looks with heartsick sighs. One fleeting moment of joy costs twenty sleepless, weary, tedious nights. If you happen to win, maybe it’s an unlucky prize. If you lose, then all you’ve won is painful work. Either way, it’s foolishness bought with your intelligence, or else intelligence beaten by foolishness.
PROTEUS. So, going by your argument, you’re calling me a fool.
VALENTINE. So, going by your situation, I’m afraid you’ll turn out to be one.
PROTEUS. It’s love you’re picking at. I’m not Love.
VALENTINE. Love is your master, because he masters you. And I think a man who lets a fool put him in harness shouldn’t go down in history as wise.
PROTEUS. But writers say that just as the gnawing cankerworm lives in the sweetest bud, gnawing love lives in the finest minds of all.

VALENTINE. And writers also say that the earliest bud gets eaten by the cankerworm before it ever blooms. In the same way, love turns a young, tender mind to foolishness. It withers in the bud, losing its green freshness in its prime, along with all the fine results it promised for the future. But why am I wasting time advising you, when you’re a devoted worshipper of foolish desire? Goodbye once more. My father is waiting for me at the harbor to see me onto the ship.
PROTEUS. And I’ll walk you there, Valentine.

VALENTINE. No, sweet Proteus. Let’s say goodbye here. Write me letters in Milan about how your love is going and whatever other news happens here while your friend is away. I’ll do the same and visit you with my letters.
PROTEUS. I wish you every happiness in Milan.
VALENTINE. The same to you at home. And so, goodbye.
[He exits.]

PROTEUS. He hunts for honor, and I hunt for love. He leaves his friends so he can bring them more honor. I leave myself, my friends, and everything for love. You, Julia, you have transformed me. You’ve made me neglect my studies and waste my time. You’ve made me fight against good advice and think the world worth nothing. You’ve made my mind weak with daydreaming and my heart sick with worry.
[Speed enters.]
SPEED. Sir Proteus, God save you. Have you seen my master?
PROTEUS. He just left here to board the ship for Milan.
SPEED. Then it’s twenty to one he’s already on board, and I’ve acted like a sheep by losing him.
PROTEUS. It’s true, a sheep very often strays if the shepherd is away for a while.
SPEED. So you conclude that my master is a shepherd, and I’m a sheep?
PROTEUS. I do.
SPEED. Well then, my horns are his horns, whether I’m awake or asleep.
PROTEUS. A stupid answer, and just right for a sheep.
SPEED. That proves I’m still a sheep.
PROTEUS. True, and your master is a shepherd.
SPEED. No, I can disprove that with an argument.
PROTEUS. I’ll have a hard time of it if I can’t prove it with another one.
SPEED. The shepherd looks for the sheep, and the sheep doesn’t look for the shepherd. But I’m looking for my master, and my master isn’t looking for me. So I’m not a sheep.

PROTEUS. The sheep follows the shepherd to get its food. The shepherd doesn’t follow the sheep to get his food. You follow your master to get your wages. Your master doesn’t follow you to get his wages. So you are a sheep.
SPEED. One more proof like that and I’ll be crying “baa”.
PROTEUS. But listen, did you give my letter to Julia?
SPEED. Yes, sir. I, a lost sheep, gave your letter to her, a laced-up tart. And she, the laced-up tart, gave me, the lost sheep, nothing for my trouble.
PROTEUS. This pasture is too small for so many sheep.
SPEED. If the field is overcrowded, you’d better slaughter her.
PROTEUS. No, you’ve wandered off there. It would be better to pen you up in the pound.
SPEED. No, sir, less than a pound in money will pay me well enough for carrying your letter.
PROTEUS. You misunderstand. I mean the pound where stray animals are penned, a pinfold.
SPEED. From a pound down to a pin? Fold it over and over, and it’s still three times too little for carrying a letter to your lover.
PROTEUS. But what did she say?
SPEED. [He nods his head.] Ay.
PROTEUS. A nod and an “Ay”. Why, put together that makes “noddy”, an idiot.
SPEED. You misunderstood, sir. I say she nodded, and you ask me whether she nodded, and I say “Ay”.
PROTEUS. And put together, that makes “noddy”.
SPEED. Well, since you’ve gone to the trouble of putting it together, keep it as payment for your trouble.
PROTEUS. No, no, you can have it for delivering the letter.
SPEED. Well, I see I’ll just have to put up with you.
PROTEUS. Why, sir, how are you putting up with me?
SPEED. Well, sir, I carried the letter very properly, and all I got for my trouble was the word “noddy”.
PROTEUS. Damn me, you have a quick wit.
SPEED. And yet it can’t catch up with your slow purse.
PROTEUS. Come on, come on, open up the matter. In short, what did she say?
SPEED. Open your purse, so the money and the matter can both be delivered at the same time.
PROTEUS. [He gives Speed a coin.] All right, sir, here’s something for your trouble. What did she say?
SPEED. Honestly, sir, I don’t think you’ll win her easily.
PROTEUS. Why? Could you tell that much from her?

SPEED. Sir, I couldn’t get anything at all from her. No, not even a gold coin for delivering your letter. And since she was so hard on me, the one who carried your feelings to her, I’m afraid she’ll be just as hard on you when you tell her your feelings yourself. Don’t give her any gifts except stones, because she’s as hard as steel.
PROTEUS. What, she said nothing?

SPEED. No, not even “Take this for your trouble.” To show how generous you are, I thank you. You’ve tipped me a sixpence. In return for it, from now on carry your letters yourself. And so, sir, I’ll give my master your regards.
PROTEUS. Go on, go, get out of here and save your master’s ship from wreck. It can’t sink with you on board, because you’re destined for a drier death on land, by hanging.
[Speed exits.]
I have to send a better messenger. I’m afraid my Julia wouldn’t stoop to read my letter if she got it from such a worthless courier.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. The garden of Julia’s house
paragraphs: [Julia and Lucetta enter.]
JULIA. But tell me, Lucetta, now that we’re alone, would you advise me to fall in love?
LUCETTA. Yes, madam, as long as you don’t stumble into it carelessly.
JULIA. Of all the fine gentlemen who come to see me and talk with me every day, which one do you think most deserves my love?
LUCETTA. Please name them for me, and I’ll tell you what I think, as far as my shallow, simple judgment goes.
JULIA. What do you think of handsome Sir Eglamour?
LUCETTA. I think he’s a well-spoken, neat, and elegant knight. But if I were you, he’d never be mine.
JULIA. What do you think of rich Mercatio?
LUCETTA. I think well of his money, but of the man himself, only so-so.
JULIA. What do you think of gentle Proteus?
LUCETTA. Lord, Lord, look how foolish we can be!
JULIA. What’s this? Why do you get so worked up at his name?
LUCETTA. Forgive me, dear madam. It’s a real shame for a lowly person like me to pass judgment on fine gentlemen like this.
JULIA. Why not on Proteus, as on all the others?
LUCETTA. Then here it is: of many good men, I think he’s the best.
JULIA. Your reason?
LUCETTA. I have no reason except a woman’s reason: I think so because I think so.
JULIA. And would you have me throw my love on him?
LUCETTA. Yes, if you didn’t think your love would be thrown away.
JULIA. But of all of them, he’s the one who has never tried to win me.
LUCETTA. And yet of all of them, I think he loves you best.
JULIA. He says so little that it shows his love is small.
LUCETTA. A fire that’s kept most tightly shut in burns the hottest.
JULIA. People who don’t show their love don’t really love.
LUCETTA. Oh, the people who love least are the ones who tell everyone about their love.
JULIA. I wish I knew what he was thinking.
LUCETTA. Read this paper, madam.
[She gives her a letter.]
JULIA. To Julia—tell me, who is it from?
LUCETTA. What’s inside will tell you.
JULIA. Tell me, tell me, who gave it to you?
LUCETTA. Sir Valentine’s servant boy, and I think it was sent by Proteus. He meant to give it to you, but I happened to be in his way, so I took it in your name. Please forgive me for that.

JULIA. Now, by my modesty, what a fine go-between you are! How dare you take in flirtatious letters? You whisper and plot against my youth and innocence! Believe me, it’s a very worthy job, and you’re just the right official for it. There, take the paper. Make sure it gets sent back, or else never come back into my sight again.
LUCETTA. Pleading for love deserves a better reward than hatred.
JULIA. Will you go away?
LUCETTA. I will, so you can think it over.
[She exits.]

JULIA. And yet I wish I had looked over the letter. It would be shameful to call her back and beg her to commit the very fault I scolded her for. What a fool she is! She knows I’m a young unmarried woman, so why didn’t she force the letter on me? Modest girls say “No” to things they’d like the man offering them to take as “Yes”. Damn it, how contrary this foolish love is! It’s like a cranky baby that scratches its nurse and then, all humble, kisses the rod that punished it. How rudely I scolded Lucetta away, when I really wanted her to stay! How angrily I taught my face to frown, when inner joy was forcing my heart to smile! As penance, I have to call Lucetta back and ask forgiveness for my foolishness. Hey there! Lucetta!
[Lucetta enters.]
LUCETTA. What does your ladyship want?
JULIA. Is it nearly dinner time?
LUCETTA. I wish it were, so you could take out your temper on your food instead of on your maid.
[She drops the letter and picks it up again.]
JULIA. What was that you picked up so carefully?
LUCETTA. Nothing.
JULIA. Then why did you bend down?
LUCETTA. To pick up a paper I dropped.
JULIA. And that paper is nothing?
LUCETTA. Nothing that concerns me.
JULIA. Then leave it lying there for whoever it does concern.
LUCETTA. Madam, it won’t lie to the one it concerns, unless someone reads it falsely.
JULIA. Some lover of yours has written to you in rhyme.
LUCETTA. So that I could sing it to a tune, madam. Give me a note to start on. Your ladyship can set—
JULIA. As little value on such trifles as possible. You’d better sing it to the tune of “Light o’ Love”.
LUCETTA. It’s too heavy for such a light tune.
JULIA. Heavy? Then I suppose it has some burden, a refrain?
LUCETTA. Yes, and it would sound lovely if you sang it.
JULIA. And why not you?
LUCETTA. I can’t reach that high.
JULIA. Let’s see your song. [She takes the letter.] What’s this, you hussy!
LUCETTA. Keep that tone if you mean to sing it to the end. And yet I don’t think I like this tune.
JULIA. You don’t?
LUCETTA. No, madam, it’s too sharp.
JULIA. You, hussy, are too cheeky.
LUCETTA. No, now you’re too flat, and you’re spoiling the harmony with too harsh a melody line. All your song needs is a middle part, a tenor, to fill it out.
JULIA. The middle part is drowned out by your unruly bass.
LUCETTA. That’s right, I’m speaking up for Proteus, taking his side in the game.

JULIA. This babbling won’t bother me anymore. What a fuss over a declaration of love! [She tears up the letter.] Go on, get out of here, and leave the pieces lying there. You’d like to be handling them just to make me angry.
LUCETTA. She’s acting like she doesn’t care, but she’d be very happy to be made angry by another letter like it.
[She exits.]

JULIA. No, I wish I were made angry by the same one! Oh, hateful hands, to tear such loving words! You’re cruel wasps, feeding on such sweet honey and then killing the bees that make it with your stings! I’ll kiss each separate scrap to make up for it. Look, here it says kind Julia. Unkind Julia! To pay you back for your ingratitude, I throw your name against the bruising stones and trample scornfully on your disdain. And here it says love-wounded Proteus. Poor wounded name, my breast will be your bed and keep you until your wound is completely healed. And so I probe the wound with a healing kiss. But Proteus was written down two or three times. Be still, good wind, don’t blow a single word away until I’ve found every letter in the letter except my own name. Let some whirlwind carry that to a jagged, frightening, overhanging rock and throw it from there into the raging sea. Look, here his name is written twice in one line: poor forlorn Proteus, passionate Proteus, to the sweet Julia. I’ll tear that part away. And yet I won’t, since he pairs it so prettily with his own sorrowful names. So I’ll fold them on top of each other. Now kiss, hug, fight, do whatever you want.
[Lucetta enters.]
LUCETTA. Madam, dinner is ready, and your father is waiting.
JULIA. Well, let’s go.
LUCETTA. What, are these papers going to lie here like tattletales?
JULIA. If you care about them, you’d better pick them up.
LUCETTA. No, I got scolded for putting them down. Still, they won’t lie here, or they’ll catch cold.
[She picks up the pieces of the letter.]
JULIA. I see you’ve got quite a craving for them.
LUCETTA. Yes, madam, you can say whatever you see. I see things too, even though you think I have my eyes shut.
JULIA. Come on, come on, will you please go?
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — The same. A room in Antonio’s house
paragraphs: [Antonio and Pantino enter.]
ANTONIO. Tell me, Pantino, what was that serious conversation my brother kept you in at the cloister?
PANTINO. It was about his nephew Proteus, your son.
ANTONIO. Why, what about him?

PANTINO. He was surprised that your lordship lets him spend his youth at home. Other men, with far less standing, send their sons out to make their way in the world. Some go to the wars to try their luck there. Some go to discover faraway islands. Some go to the universities to study. He said your son Proteus was fit for any or all of these pursuits. He asked me to urge you not to let him spend his time at home any longer. It would be a great disadvantage to him when he’s older to have done no traveling in his youth.

ANTONIO. You don’t need to push me much on that, because I’ve been hammering at it all this month. I’ve thought carefully about how he’s wasting his time. He can’t become a complete man without being tested and taught by the world. Experience is gained by hard work and perfected by the swift passing of time. So tell me, where would be the best place to send him?
PANTINO. I think your lordship knows that his friend, young Valentine, serves the Emperor at his royal court.
ANTONIO. I know that well.

PANTINO. I think it would be good if your lordship sent him there. He can practice jousting and tournaments there, hear refined conversation, and talk with noblemen. He’ll see every activity worthy of his youth and his noble birth.
ANTONIO. I like your advice. You’ve advised me well. And to show you how much I like it, I’ll put it into action. I’ll send him to the Emperor’s court as quickly as possible.
PANTINO. If you please, tomorrow Don Alphonso and some other well-respected gentlemen are traveling to greet the Emperor and offer him their service.
ANTONIO. Good company. Proteus will go with them.
[Proteus enters, reading a letter.]
And just in time! Now we’ll tell him about it.

PROTEUS. Sweet love, sweet words, sweet life! Here is her handwriting, the messenger of her heart. Here is her vow of love, the pledge of her honor. Oh, if only our fathers would approve of our love and seal our happiness with their consent. Oh, heavenly Julia!
ANTONIO. What’s this? What letter are you reading there?
PROTEUS. If it please your lordship, it’s a word or two of greetings sent from Valentine. A friend who came from him delivered it.
ANTONIO. Let me have the letter. Let me see what the news is.

PROTEUS. There’s no news, my lord, except that he writes about how happily he lives, how well loved he is, and how the Emperor favors him every day. He wishes I were with him to share his good fortune.
ANTONIO. And how do you feel about his wish?
PROTEUS. Like someone who relies on your lordship’s will, and not on Valentine’s friendly wish.

ANTONIO. My will happens to agree with his wish. Don’t be surprised that I’m acting so suddenly, because what I want, I want, and that’s the end of it. I’ve decided that you’ll spend some time with Valentine at the Emperor’s court. Whatever allowance he gets from his family, you’ll get the same from me. Be ready to leave tomorrow. Don’t make excuses, because my mind is made up.
PROTEUS. My lord, I can’t get ready so soon. Please think it over for a day or two.
ANTONIO. Whatever you need will be sent after you. No more delay. You must leave tomorrow. Come on, Pantino, I’ll put you to work hurrying along his departure.
[Antonio and Pantino exit.]

PROTEUS. So I avoided the fire because I was afraid of getting burned, and threw myself into the sea, where I’m drowning. I was afraid to show my father Julia’s letter in case he objected to my love. And he has used my own excuse as the very weapon to strike hardest against my love. Oh, how this springtime of love is like the unreliable glory of an April day! One moment it shows all the beauty of the sun, and the next a cloud takes it all away.
[Pantino enters.]
PANTINO. Sir Proteus, your father is calling for you. He’s in a hurry, so please go.
PROTEUS. Well, this is how it is: my heart agrees to go, and yet a thousand times over it answers “No”.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Milan. A room in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Valentine and Speed enter.]
SPEED. Sir, here’s your glove.
VALENTINE. It isn’t mine. My gloves are on.
SPEED. Well, then, this one might be yours, since it’s only one.
VALENTINE. What? Let me see it. Yes, give it to me, it’s mine. Sweet ornament that adorns a divine creature! Ah, Silvia, Silvia!
SPEED. [Calling.] Madam Silvia! Madam Silvia!
VALENTINE. What are you doing, boy?
SPEED. She can’t hear you, sir.
VALENTINE. Well, sir, who told you to call her?
SPEED. You did, sir, or else I misunderstood.
VALENTINE. Well, you’re always too pushy.
SPEED. And yet the last time I got scolded, it was for being too slow.
VALENTINE. Enough of that, sir. Tell me, do you know Madam Silvia?
SPEED. The one you’re in love with?
VALENTINE. Why, how do you know I’m in love?

SPEED. Well, by these particular signs. First, like Sir Proteus, you’ve learned to fold your arms like a sulky malcontent. You enjoy a love song, like a robin redbreast. You walk alone, like someone with the plague. You sigh, like a schoolboy who has lost his alphabet book. You weep, like a young girl who has buried her grandma. You go without food, like someone on a diet. You stay awake, like someone afraid of burglars. You whine when you talk, like a beggar on All Saints’ Day. You used to crow like a rooster when you laughed. You used to walk like a lion. When you went without food, it was right after a big dinner. When you looked sad, it was because you were short of money. And now you’re so transformed by a mistress that when I look at you, I can hardly believe you’re my master.
VALENTINE. Can people see all these things in me?
SPEED. They can all be seen from outside you.
VALENTINE. Outside me? That’s impossible.

SPEED. Outside you? No, that’s certain, because if you weren’t such a fool, nobody else would notice them. But you’re so wrapped up in these follies that they’re inside you. They shine through you like the water in a doctor’s urine flask. Every eye that sees you becomes a physician who can diagnose your disease.
VALENTINE. But tell me, do you know my lady Silvia?
SPEED. The one you stare at like that while she sits at supper?
VALENTINE. You noticed that? Yes, she’s the one I mean.
SPEED. Well, sir, I don’t know her.
VALENTINE. You recognize her from my staring at her, and yet you don’t know her?
SPEED. Isn’t she ugly, sir?
VALENTINE. She’s not so much beautiful, boy, as gracious and charming.
SPEED. Sir, I know that well enough.
VALENTINE. What do you know?
SPEED. That she isn’t as beautiful as you, sir, find her charming.
VALENTINE. I mean that her beauty is exquisite, but her graciousness is infinite.
SPEED. That’s because the one is painted on with makeup, and the other is beyond counting.
VALENTINE. What do you mean, painted? And what do you mean, beyond counting?
SPEED. Well, sir, she’s so painted up to make herself look beautiful that no man takes her beauty into account.
VALENTINE. What do you take me for? I take her beauty into account.
SPEED. You haven’t seen her since she became deformed.
VALENTINE. How long has she been deformed?
SPEED. Ever since you fell in love with her.
VALENTINE. I’ve loved her ever since I first saw her, and I still see that she’s beautiful.
SPEED. If you love her, you can’t see her.
VALENTINE. Why?
SPEED. Because Love is blind. Oh, I wish you had my eyes! Or I wish your own eyes had the sight they used to have when you scolded Sir Proteus for going around without his garters!
VALENTINE. What would I see then?

SPEED. Your own present foolishness and her extreme ugliness. Because he, being in love, couldn’t see well enough to tie up his stockings. And you, being in love, can’t see well enough to put your stockings on.
VALENTINE. Then I suppose you’re in love, boy, because yesterday morning you couldn’t see well enough to wipe my shoes.
SPEED. True, sir, I was in love with my bed. Thank you, you beat me for my love, which makes me bolder about scolding you for yours.
VALENTINE. In short, I stand devoted to her.
SPEED. I wish you’d sit down, so your devotion would stop standing up.
VALENTINE. Last night she asked me to write some verses to someone she loves.
SPEED. And have you?
VALENTINE. I have.
SPEED. Aren’t they badly written, with limping lines?
VALENTINE. No, boy, they’re as good as I can make them. Quiet, here she comes.
[Silvia enters.]
SPEED. [Aside.] Oh, what a great puppet show! Oh, what a marvelous puppet! Now he’ll speak her lines for her, like the puppet master.
VALENTINE. Madam and mistress, a thousand good mornings to you.
SPEED. [Aside.] Oh, and good evening to you too! What a million manners he’s got.
SILVIA. Sir Valentine, my servant, two thousand good mornings to you.
SPEED. [Aside.] He should be paying her interest, and instead she pays it to him.
VALENTINE. As you asked me to, I’ve written your letter to that secret, nameless friend of yours. I was very reluctant to do it, and did it only out of duty to your ladyship.
[He gives her a letter.]
SILVIA. Thank you, kind servant. It’s very skillfully done, like a real scholar’s work.
VALENTINE. Believe me, madam, it was hard work. Since I don’t know who it’s going to, I had to write at random, with a lot of uncertainty.
SILVIA. Maybe you think it was too much trouble to go to?
VALENTINE. No, madam. If it helps you, I’ll write a thousand times as much, if you order me to. And yet—
SILVIA. What a pretty place to stop. Well, I can guess what comes next. And yet I won’t say it. And yet I don’t care. And yet take this back.
[She offers him the letter.]
And yet I thank you, though I don’t intend to trouble you any more from now on.
SPEED. [Aside.] And yet you will. And there’s another “yet”.
VALENTINE. What do you mean, your ladyship? Don’t you like it?
SILVIA. Yes, yes, the lines are very cleverly written. But since you wrote them unwillingly, take them back. No, take them.
[She offers the letter again.]
VALENTINE. Madam, they’re for you.
SILVIA. Yes, yes, you wrote them, sir, because I asked you to, but I don’t want them. They’re for you. I would have liked them to be written with more feeling.
VALENTINE. If you like, I’ll write your ladyship another one.
SILVIA. And when it’s written, read it over for my sake. If you like it, fine. If you don’t, well, fine too.
VALENTINE. If I like it, madam? What then?
SILVIA. Why, if you like it, keep it as payment for your work. And so good morning, servant.
[She exits.]

SPEED. [Aside.] Oh, what a joke, hidden, mysterious, invisible—about as invisible as a nose on a man’s face or a weathervane on a steeple! My master is courting her, and she has taught her suitor, who is her pupil, to become her teacher. Oh, what a brilliant trick! Was a better one ever heard of? My master, playing the secretary, has ended up writing the letter to himself!
VALENTINE. What’s this, sir? What are you arguing about with yourself?
SPEED. No, I was making rhymes. You’re the one who has the reason.
VALENTINE. The reason to do what?
SPEED. To be a spokesman for Madam Silvia.
VALENTINE. To whom?
SPEED. To yourself. Why, she’s wooing you indirectly, by a figure of speech.
VALENTINE. What figure of speech?
SPEED. By a letter, I should say.
VALENTINE. But she hasn’t written to me.
SPEED. Why would she need to, when she’s made you write to yourself? Don’t you get the joke?
VALENTINE. No, believe me.
SPEED. There’s no believing you, sir, that’s for sure. But did you notice she was in earnest?
VALENTINE. She gave me nothing in earnest, except an angry word.
SPEED. Why, she’s given you a letter.
VALENTINE. That’s the letter I wrote to her friend.
SPEED. And she’s delivered that letter, and that’s the end of it.
VALENTINE. I wish it were no worse than that.

SPEED. I promise you, it’s just as good as that. You’ve often written to her. And she, out of modesty, or because she didn’t have spare time, couldn’t write back. Or else she was afraid some messenger would reveal her feelings. So she has taught her beloved to write to her lover himself. I’m saying all this word for word, because I read it in print. Why are you lost in thought, sir? It’s dinner time.
VALENTINE. I’ve already eaten.

SPEED. Yes, but listen, sir. Love may be like the chameleon that can feed on air, but I’m someone who is nourished by food, and I’d really like something to eat. Oh, don’t be like your mistress! Be moved, be moved—to dinner.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — Verona. A room in Julia’s house
paragraphs: [Proteus and Julia enter.]
PROTEUS. Be patient, gentle Julia.
JULIA. I have to be, since there’s nothing to be done about it.
PROTEUS. As soon as I possibly can, I’ll come back.
JULIA. If you don’t turn to someone else, you’ll come back sooner. Keep this as a reminder of your Julia.
[She gives him a ring.]
PROTEUS. Why, then we’ll trade. Here, you take this.
[He gives her a ring.]
JULIA. And let’s seal the deal with a holy kiss.

PROTEUS. Here’s my hand as a pledge that I’ll stay true. If an hour ever slips by in my day when I don’t sigh for you, Julia, then let some terrible disaster torment me in the very next hour for forgetting my love. My father is waiting for me to come. Don’t answer. The tide is turning now—no, not your tide of tears. That tide would hold me here longer than I should stay. Julia, goodbye.
[Julia exits.]
What, she’s gone without a word? Yes, that’s how true love should behave. It can’t speak, because truth has better deeds than words to honor it.
[Pantino enters.]
PANTINO. Sir Proteus, they’re waiting for you.
PROTEUS. Go on, I’m coming, I’m coming. Alas, this parting leaves poor lovers speechless.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Lance enters with his dog, Crab.]

LANCE. No, it’ll be an hour before I’m done crying. All the Lances have this same weakness. I’ve received my share of the inheritance, like the prodigal son—the prodigious son, I mean—and I’m going with Sir Proteus to the Emperor’s court. I think my dog Crab is the sourest-tempered dog alive. My mother was weeping, my father wailing, my sister crying, our maid howling, our cat wringing her hands, and our whole house was in a terrible state. And yet this cruel-hearted mutt didn’t shed a single tear. He’s a stone, a real pebble, and has no more pity in him than a dog. A Jew would have wept to see our parting. Why, my grandma, who has no eyes, you see, wept herself blind when I left. No, I’ll show you how it went. This shoe is my father. No, this left shoe is my father. No, no, this left shoe is my mother. No, that can’t be right either. Yes, it is, it is—it has the worse sole. This shoe with the hole in it is my mother, and this one is my father. Damn it, there it is. Now, sir, this stick is my sister, because, you see, she’s as white as a lily and as thin as a wand. This hat is Nan, our maid. I’m the dog. No, the dog is himself, and I’m the dog. Oh, the dog is me, and I’m myself. Yes, that’s it, that’s it. Now I come to my father: “Father, your blessing.” Now the shoe shouldn’t be able to say a word, it’s crying so hard. Now I kiss my father. Well, he keeps on crying. Now I come to my mother. Oh, if only she could speak now like a woman out of her mind with grief! Well, I kiss her. Why, there it is—that’s my mother’s breath exactly. Now I come to my sister. Listen to the moaning she makes. And the whole time the dog doesn’t shed a tear or say a word. But look how I settle the dust with my tears.
[Pantino enters.]

PANTINO. Lance, go, go! Get on board! Your master has set sail, and you have to row after him in a hurry. What’s the matter? Why are you crying, man? Go, you ass. You’ll miss the tide if you wait any longer.
LANCE. It doesn’t matter if the tied one were lost, because it’s the unkindest tied creature that any man ever tied up.
PANTINO. What’s the unkindest tide?
LANCE. Why, the one that’s tied up here, Crab, my dog.

PANTINO. Come on, man, I mean you’ll miss the high tide. And if you miss the tide, you’ll miss your voyage. And if you miss your voyage, you’ll lose your master. And if you lose your master, you’ll lose your job. And if you lose your job—why are you covering my mouth?
LANCE. Because I’m afraid you’ll lose your tongue.
PANTINO. Where would I lose my tongue?
LANCE. In your tale.
PANTINO. In your tail, you mean!

LANCE. Miss the tide, the trip, the master, the job and the tied-up dog? Listen, man, if the river ran dry, my tears alone could fill it. If the wind dropped, my sighs would be enough to push the boat along.
PANTINO. Come on, come away, man. I was sent to call you.
LANCE. Sir, call me whatever you dare.
PANTINO. Will you go?
LANCE. Well, I’ll go.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 4 — Milan. A room in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Valentine, Silvia, Thurio and Speed enter.]
SILVIA. Servant!
VALENTINE. Mistress?
SPEED. Master, Sir Thurio is frowning at you.
VALENTINE. Yes, boy, it’s because of love.
SPEED. Not love of you.
VALENTINE. Of my mistress, then.
SPEED. It would be a good idea to knock him down.
SILVIA. Servant, you’re sad.
VALENTINE. Yes, madam, I seem to be.
THURIO. Do you seem to be what you’re not?
VALENTINE. Maybe I do.
THURIO. So do fakes.
VALENTINE. So do you.
THURIO. What do I seem to be that I’m not?
VALENTINE. Wise.
THURIO. What proof do you have of the opposite?
VALENTINE. Your foolishness.
THURIO. And where do you see my foolishness written down?
VALENTINE. I see it written in your jacket.
THURIO. My jacket is a doublet.
VALENTINE. Well, then, I’ll double your foolishness.
THURIO. What!
SILVIA. What, are you angry, Sir Thurio? Are you changing color?
VALENTINE. Let him be, madam. He’s a kind of chameleon.
THURIO. One that would rather feed on your blood than live on your air.
VALENTINE. You’ve said your piece, sir.
THURIO. Yes, sir, and I’m done too, for now.
VALENTINE. I know that well, sir. You always finish before you start.
SILVIA. A fine volley of words, gentlemen, and quickly fired off.
VALENTINE. It is indeed, madam, and we thank the one who supplied the ammunition.
SILVIA. Who is that, servant?
VALENTINE. You yourself, sweet lady, because you lit the fuse. Sir Thurio borrows his wit from your ladyship’s looks. Then he generously spends what he borrows while he’s in your company.
THURIO. Sir, if you trade word for word with me, I’ll bankrupt your wit.

VALENTINE. I know that well, sir. You have a whole treasury of words and, I think, no other wealth to give your servants. You can tell by their threadbare uniforms that they live on nothing but your empty words.
SILVIA. No more, gentlemen, no more. Here comes my father.
[The Duke enters.]
DUKE. Well, my daughter Silvia, you’re under heavy siege. Sir Valentine, your father is in good health. What would you say to a letter from your family with lots of good news?
VALENTINE. My lord, I’d be grateful to any messenger bringing happy news from there.
DUKE. Do you know Don Antonio, from your hometown?
VALENTINE. Yes, my good lord, I know the gentleman. He’s a man of worth and is highly respected, and he deserves his good reputation.
DUKE. Doesn’t he have a son?
VALENTINE. Yes, my good lord, a son who well deserves the honor and respect of a father like that.
DUKE. Do you know him well?

VALENTINE. I know him as well as I know myself, because we’ve spent our time together since we were babies. I myself have been a lazy truant. I’ve neglected the precious opportunity of my youth to dress my later years in angelic perfection. But Sir Proteus, for that’s his name, has made good use of his days and taken full advantage of them. He is young in years, but old in experience. His head is still green, but his judgment is ripe. In a word, all the praise I’m giving him now falls far short of his worth. He is perfect in body and in mind, with every fine quality that does a gentleman credit.

DUKE. Upon my word, sir, if he lives up to this, he’s as worthy of an empress’s love as he is fit to be an emperor’s adviser. Well, sir, this gentleman has come to me with recommendations from powerful rulers. He intends to spend some time here. I imagine this isn’t unwelcome news to you.
VALENTINE. If I could have wished for anything, it would have been him.
DUKE. Then welcome him as he deserves. Silvia, I’m talking to you, and to you, Sir Thurio. As for Valentine, I don’t need to urge him to do it. I’ll send him in to you right away.
[He exits.]
VALENTINE. This is the gentleman I told your ladyship about. He would have come with me, except that his mistress kept his eyes locked up in her crystal gaze.
SILVIA. Maybe she has set them free now, after taking some other pledge of his loyalty.
VALENTINE. No, I’m sure she still holds them prisoner.
SILVIA. Well, then he must be blind. And if he’s blind, how could he see his way here to find you?
VALENTINE. Why, lady, Love has twenty pairs of eyes.
THURIO. They say that Love doesn’t have any eyes at all.
VALENTINE. Not to see lovers like you, Thurio. Love can shut its eyes to an ugly sight.
SILVIA. Stop it, stop it. Here comes the gentleman.
[Proteus enters.]
VALENTINE. Welcome, dear Proteus! Mistress, I beg you, confirm his welcome with some special sign of favor.
SILVIA. If this is the man you have so often wished to hear from, his worth guarantees him a welcome here.
VALENTINE. It is, my lady. Sweet lady, take him on as my fellow servant to your ladyship.
SILVIA. I am too lowly a mistress for so lofty a servant.
PROTEUS. Not so, sweet lady. I am too lowly a servant to deserve even a glance from such a worthy mistress.
VALENTINE. Stop talking about what you are unfit for. Sweet lady, accept him as your servant.
PROTEUS. The only thing I will boast of is my devotion to duty.
SILVIA. And duty has never yet gone without its reward. Servant, you are welcome to a worthless mistress.
PROTEUS. I would fight to the death any man who said that, except you.
SILVIA. Said that you are welcome?
PROTEUS. Said that you are worthless.
[A Servant enters.]
SERVANT. Madam, my lord your father wants to speak with you.
SILVIA. I am at his service.
[The Servant exits.]
Come with me, Sir Thurio.—Once more, my new servant, welcome. I’ll leave you two to talk about matters at home. When you are finished, we expect to hear from you.
PROTEUS. We will both wait on your ladyship.
[Silvia and Thurio exit.]
VALENTINE. Now tell me, how is everyone back where you came from?
PROTEUS. Your friends are well, and they send you their warm regards.
VALENTINE. And how are yours?
PROTEUS. They were all in good health when I left.
VALENTINE. How is your lady? And how is your love going?
PROTEUS. My love stories used to bore you. I know you take no pleasure in talk about love.

VALENTINE. Yes, Proteus, but that life has changed now. I have done penance for scorning Love. His lofty, domineering thoughts have punished me with bitter fasting, with groans of repentance, with tears every night and aching sighs every day. To take revenge for my contempt, Love has chased sleep from my captive eyes and set them to keep watch over my own heart’s sorrow. Oh, gentle Proteus, Love is a mighty lord. He has humbled me so much that I admit there is no misery like his punishment, and no joy on earth like serving him. Now I want no conversation unless it is about love. Now I can make my breakfast, lunch, dinner and bedtime out of the bare word love alone.
PROTEUS. That’s enough. I can read your fortune in your eyes. Was that the idol you worship so much?
VALENTINE. That’s her. Isn’t she a heavenly saint?
PROTEUS. No, but she is an earthly model of perfection.
VALENTINE. Call her divine.
PROTEUS. I will not flatter her.
VALENTINE. Oh, flatter me, then, because love loves to hear praise.
PROTEUS. When I was sick with love, you gave me bitter medicine. Now I must give you the same.
VALENTINE. Then tell the truth about her. If she is not divine, at least let her be an angel of high rank, ruling over every creature on earth.
PROTEUS. Except my own mistress.
VALENTINE. My friend, make no exceptions, unless you want to take exception to my love.
PROTEUS. Don’t I have good reason to rank my own lady first?

VALENTINE. And I will help you raise her up too. She will be granted this great honor: to carry my lady’s train. That way the lowly earth won’t get the chance to steal a kiss from Silvia’s gown. Otherwise the earth might grow so proud of that favor that it would refuse to nourish the summer flowers, and make harsh winter last forever.
PROTEUS. Why, Valentine, what is all this bragging?
VALENTINE. Forgive me, Proteus. Everything I can say is nothing compared to her. Her worth makes other worthy women look like nothing. She is unique.
PROTEUS. Then leave her alone.

VALENTINE. Not for the world! Why, man, she is mine. Having such a jewel makes me as rich as twenty seas would be if all their sand were pearls, their water nectar and their rocks pure gold. Forgive me for not paying attention to you. You can see I am infatuated with my love. My foolish rival, whom her father favors only because his estates are so huge, has gone off with her. I must follow them, because love, as you know, is full of jealousy.
PROTEUS. But does she love you?

VALENTINE. Yes, and we are engaged. More than that, we have set the hour of our marriage and every clever detail of our escape. I am to climb up to her window on a ladder made of ropes. We have planned and agreed on every means to my happiness. Good Proteus, come with me to my room and help me with your advice in these matters.
PROTEUS. Go on ahead, and I will find you there. First I must go down to the harbor to unload some things I need to use. Then I’ll come and join you right away.
VALENTINE. Will you hurry?
PROTEUS. I will.
[Valentine exits.]

Just as one fire drives out another fire’s heat, or as one nail forcibly knocks out another, the memory of my old love has been completely wiped out by a new one. Is it my own eyes, or Valentine’s praise of her? Is it her true perfection, or my own disloyalty, that makes me reason so unreasonably? She is beautiful. So is Julia, whom I love—whom I did love. My love for Julia has melted now. Like a wax figure held up to a fire, it no longer keeps the shape it once had. I feel that my devotion to Valentine has cooled, and that I don’t love him the way I used to. Oh, but I love his lady far too much, and that’s why I love him so little. How much more will I adore her once I really know her, when I have started loving her without thinking at all? So far I have only seen her outside, like a painted picture, and even that has dazzled the light of my reason. When I see all her inner perfections, I am bound to go completely blind. If I can stop this wayward love, I will. If not, I will use all my cleverness to win her.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 5 — The same. A street
paragraphs: [Speed and Lance enter, with Lance’s dog Crab.]
SPEED. Lance, on my honor, welcome to Milan!

LANCE. Don’t perjure yourself, sweet boy, because I am not welcome. I always count on this: a man is never ruined until he is hanged, and he is never welcome anywhere until he has paid the bill and the landlady says “Welcome.”

SPEED. Come on, you lunatic. I’ll go to the pub with you right now. There, for one bill of five pennies, you’ll get five thousand welcomes. But tell me, how did your master say goodbye to Madam Julia?
LANCE. Well, after they embraced in earnest, they parted very nicely as if it were a joke.
SPEED. But is she going to marry him?
LANCE. No.
SPEED. What then? Is he going to marry her?
LANCE. No, not that either.
SPEED. What, have they broken up?
LANCE. No, they are both as whole and sound as a fish.
SPEED. Well then, how do things stand between them?
LANCE. Well, like this: when things stand up well for him, they stand well for her too.
SPEED. What an ass you are! I don’t understand you.
LANCE. What a blockhead you are, not to understand! Even my walking stick understands me.
SPEED. Understands what you say?
LANCE. Yes, and what I do too. Look, I’ll just lean on it, and my stick stands under me.
SPEED. It does stand under you, sure enough.
LANCE. Well, stand-under and under-stand are the same thing.
SPEED. But tell me honestly, will they get married?
LANCE. Ask my dog. If he says “Yes,” they will. If he says “No,” they will. If he wags his tail and says nothing, they will.
SPEED. So the conclusion is that they will.
LANCE. You’ll never get a secret like that out of me except through a riddle.
SPEED. I’m glad I got it that way, then. But Lance, what do you say to the news that my master has become a remarkable lover?
LANCE. I never knew him to be anything else.
SPEED. Anything else than what?
LANCE. A remarkable lump of a fool, just as you describe him.
SPEED. Why, you bastard of an ass, you’ve misunderstood me.
LANCE. Why, you fool, I didn’t mean you. I meant your master.
SPEED. I tell you, my master has become a passionate, burning lover.
LANCE. Well, I tell you, I don’t care if he burns himself up in love. If you want, come with me to the pub. If not, you are a Hebrew, a Jew, and you don’t deserve to be called a Christian.
SPEED. Why?
LANCE. Because you don’t have enough Christian charity in you to go drink ale with a Christian. Will you come?
SPEED. I’m at your service.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 6 — The same. The Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Proteus enters alone.]

PROTEUS. If I leave my Julia, I will be breaking my oath. If I love fair Silvia, I will be breaking my oath. If I wrong my friend, I will be breaking my oath even worse. And the very same power that first made me swear is now pushing me into this triple betrayal. Love made me swear, and now Love makes me break my word. Oh, tempting Love, if you have sinned, teach me, the subject you tempted, how to excuse it. At first I adored a twinkling star, but now I worship a heavenly sun. Careless vows can be carefully broken. A man lacks sense if he lacks the determination to teach his mind to trade worse for better. Shame on you, disrespectful tongue, for calling her worse. You have so often ranked her above all others, swearing twenty thousand oaths on your soul. I cannot stop loving, and yet I do stop. But I stop loving the one I ought to love. I lose Julia, and I lose Valentine. If I keep them, I must lose myself. If I lose them, I find something in that loss: myself instead of Valentine, and Silvia instead of Julia. I am dearer to myself than any friend is, because love always values itself most. And Silvia—heaven that made her beautiful is my witness—makes Julia look like a dark-skinned Ethiopian. I will forget that Julia is alive and remember only that my love for her is dead. I’ll treat Valentine as an enemy and set my sights on Silvia as a sweeter companion. I can’t be true to myself now without using some treachery against Valentine. Tonight he plans to climb heavenly Silvia’s bedroom window with a rope ladder. He has made me his confidant, and I am his rival. I will go at once and tell her father about their disguises and planned escape. The Duke will be furious and will banish Valentine, because he intends Thurio to marry his daughter. Once Valentine is gone, I will quickly block dull Thurio’s slow courtship with some sly trick. Love, lend me wings to carry out my plan quickly, just as you have lent me the cleverness to plot it.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 7 — Verona. A room in Julia’s house
paragraphs: [Julia and Lucetta enter.]

JULIA. Advise me, Lucetta. Gentle girl, help me. I beg you, out of kindness and love, since you are the notebook in which all my thoughts are plainly written and engraved: teach me and tell me some good way that I can travel to my loving Proteus without damaging my honor.
LUCETTA. Oh dear, the road is long and exhausting.

JULIA. A truly devoted pilgrim doesn’t get tired of walking across whole kingdoms on weak feet. Much less will a woman who has Love’s wings to fly with. And she will be even less tired when the journey is to someone so dear, someone as divinely perfect as Sir Proteus.
LUCETTA. You’d do better to wait until Proteus comes back.

JULIA. Oh, don’t you know that the sight of him is food for my soul? Take pity on the famine I have wasted away in, longing for that food for so long. If you only knew how love touches you inside, you would sooner try to light a fire with snow than try to put out the fire of love with words.
LUCETTA. I am not trying to put out the hot fire of your love. I only want to calm its extreme fury, so it doesn’t burn beyond the limits of reason.

JULIA. The more you dam it up, the more it burns. You know that a stream gliding along with a gentle murmur rages impatiently when it is blocked. But when nothing gets in the way of its smooth course, it makes sweet music over the polished stones. It gives a gentle kiss to every reed it passes on its pilgrimage. And so it wanders through many winding bends, playing happily, until it reaches the wild ocean. So let me go, and don’t block my course. I’ll be as patient as a gentle stream and make a game of every tiring step. I’ll keep on until the last step brings me to my love. And there I’ll rest, the way a blessed soul rests in paradise after much turmoil.
LUCETTA. But what clothes will you wear for the journey?
JULIA. Not a woman’s, because I want to avoid the advances of lecherous men. Gentle Lucetta, get me the kind of clothes that would suit a page from a good household.
LUCETTA. Well then, your ladyship will have to cut your hair.
JULIA. No, girl, I’ll tie it up with silk strings in twenty elaborate love knots. A showy style like that could suit a young man even older than I will appear to be.
LUCETTA. What style should I make your trousers, madam?
JULIA. That question makes as much sense as asking a man, “Tell me, my good lord, how wide will you wear your hoop skirt?” Why, make them in whatever style you like best, Lucetta.
LUCETTA. You will have to have them with a codpiece, madam.
JULIA. Stop it, Lucetta, that would be ugly.
LUCETTA. Madam, puffed-out trousers aren’t worth a pin these days unless you have a codpiece to stick pins in.

JULIA. Lucetta, if you love me, get me whatever you think is right and most decent. But tell me, girl, what will people think of me for setting out on such an improper journey? I’m afraid it will cause a scandal about me.
LUCETTA. If you think so, then stay at home and don’t go.
JULIA. No, I won’t do that.

LUCETTA. Then don’t worry about disgrace. Just go. If Proteus is happy about your journey when you arrive, it doesn’t matter who is displeased that you’ve left. But I’m afraid he won’t be very pleased about it.
JULIA. That is the least of my fears, Lucetta. A thousand oaths, an ocean of his tears and endless proofs of his love guarantee that my Proteus will welcome me.
LUCETTA. Deceitful men use all those things to serve them.

JULIA. Low men, to use them for such low purposes! But truer stars ruled over Proteus’ birth. His words are binding contracts, and his oaths are as true as prophecy. His love is sincere and his thoughts are spotless. His tears are pure messengers sent from his heart. His heart is as far from deceit as heaven is from earth.
LUCETTA. I pray to heaven he turns out that way when you reach him.

JULIA. Now, if you love me, don’t do him the wrong of thinking badly of his loyalty. The only way to earn my love is to love him. Come with me to my room right now and make a list of what I need for my journey of longing. I leave everything I own at your disposal: my goods, my lands, my reputation. All I ask in return is that you get me on my way. Come on, don’t argue, but get to it at once. I can’t stand this delay.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Milan. An anteroom in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [The Duke, Thurio and Proteus enter.]
DUKE. Sir Thurio, please leave us alone for a while. We have some private matters to discuss.
[Thurio exits.]
Now tell me, Proteus, what do you want with me?

PROTEUS. My gracious lord, the law of friendship tells me to hide what I am about to reveal. But when I remember the kind favors you have done me, unworthy as I am, my sense of duty spurs me to tell you something no worldly reward could otherwise get out of me. Know this, worthy prince: my friend Sir Valentine plans to steal your daughter away tonight. I myself have been let in on the plot. I know you have decided to give her in marriage to Thurio, whom your gentle daughter hates. If she were stolen away from you like this, it would greatly trouble you in your old age. So, for the sake of my duty, I chose to block my friend’s plan. I would rather do that than keep quiet and pile on your head a load of sorrows. If nothing stopped them, those sorrows would press you down into an early grave.

DUKE. Proteus, I thank you for your honest concern. In return, ask anything of me as long as I live. I have often seen this love between them myself, perhaps when they thought I was fast asleep. Many times I have intended to ban Sir Valentine from her company and from my court. But I was afraid my jealous suspicion might be wrong and that I would disgrace the man without cause. I have always avoided that kind of rashness. So I treated him kindly, hoping to find out what you have now revealed to me. And so you can see how much I feared this: knowing that young people are easily tempted, I lock her up every night in an upper tower. I have always kept the key myself, so she cannot be carried off from there.

PROTEUS. Know this, noble lord: they have worked out a way for him to climb up to her bedroom window and bring her down on a rope ladder. The young lover has gone to fetch it now. He will come this way with it soon, and you can stop him here if you like. But, my good lord, do it so cleverly that no one guesses I revealed it. It was love for you, not hatred for my friend, that made me disclose this plan.
DUKE. On my honor, he will never know that you gave me any information about this.
PROTEUS. Goodbye, my lord. Sir Valentine is coming.
[He exits.]
[Valentine enters.]
DUKE. Sir Valentine, where are you off to in such a hurry?
VALENTINE. If it please your Grace, there is a messenger waiting to carry my letters to my friends, and I am going to give them to him.
DUKE. Are they very important?
VALENTINE. All they say is that I am healthy and happy at your court.

DUKE. No? Then it doesn’t matter. Stay with me a while. I need to discuss some matters with you that concern me closely, and you must keep them secret. You know that I have been trying to marry my daughter to my friend Sir Thurio.

VALENTINE. I know it well, my lord. And surely the match would be wealthy and honorable. Besides, the gentleman is full of virtue, generosity, merit and the qualities fitting for a wife like your beautiful daughter. Can’t your Grace persuade her to like him?

DUKE. No, believe me, she’s irritable, sulky, contrary, proud, disobedient, stubborn and lacking in duty. She neither respects the fact that she’s my child nor fears me as if I were her father. And I can tell you this: after careful thought, this pride of hers has drawn my love away from her. I thought the rest of my old age would be cared for by her dutiful love as a daughter. Instead, I’m now fully resolved to take a wife myself and throw her out to whoever will take her in. Then let her beauty be her wedding dowry, since she doesn’t value me or my possessions.
VALENTINE. What would your Grace like me to do about this?

DUKE. There’s a lady here from Verona whom I’m fond of. But she’s fussy and shy, and she thinks nothing of my old man’s eloquence. So I’d like you to be my tutor. It’s been a long time since I’ve courted anyone, and anyway the fashions have changed since then. Teach me how and in what way I should carry myself so that her sun-bright eyes will notice me.
VALENTINE. Win her with gifts if she doesn’t care for words. Silent jewels, speechless as they are, often move a woman’s heart more than lively words do.
DUKE. But she turned up her nose at a present I sent her.

VALENTINE. A woman sometimes scorns what pleases her most. Send her another one, and never give up on her. Scorn at the beginning makes the love that comes later all the greater. If she frowns, it isn’t because she hates you. It’s rather to make you love her more. If she scolds you, it isn’t because she wants you to leave, because the silly things go crazy if they’re left alone. Don’t accept rejection, whatever she says. When she says “Get out of here,” she doesn’t mean “Go away!” Flatter and praise them, admire them and glorify their charms. However dark and plain they are, tell them they have the faces of angels. I say that a man who has a tongue is no man if he can’t win a woman with it.
DUKE. But the woman I mean has been promised by her family to a young gentleman of good standing. She’s kept strictly away from the company of men, so no man can get to her during the day.
VALENTINE. Well then, I would visit her at night.
DUKE. Yes, but the doors are locked and the keys are kept safe, so no man can get to her at night either.
VALENTINE. What’s to stop someone from climbing in through her window?
DUKE. Her room is high up, far from the ground, and the wall leans out so steeply that no one could climb it without obviously risking his life.
VALENTINE. Why, then a cleverly made ladder of rope, thrown up with a pair of grappling hooks, would be enough to climb another Hero’s tower, if a Leander were bold enough to risk it.
DUKE. Now, as you’re a gentleman of good blood, tell me where I can get a ladder like that.
VALENTINE. When would you use it? Please, sir, tell me that.
DUKE. Tonight. Love is like a child who wants everything he can get his hands on.
VALENTINE. I’ll get you a ladder like that by seven o’clock.
DUKE. But listen: I’ll go to her alone. What’s the best way to carry the ladder there?
VALENTINE. It will be light, my lord, so you can carry it under a cloak of any length.
DUKE. A cloak as long as yours will do the job?
VALENTINE. Yes, my good lord.
DUKE. Then let me see your cloak. I’ll get myself another one of the same length.
VALENTINE. Why, any cloak will do, my lord.
DUKE. How should I learn to wear a cloak? Please, let me try your cloak on.
[He takes Valentine’s cloak and finds a letter and a rope ladder hidden under it.]
What letter is this? What’s this? To Silvia? And here’s a tool just right for my purpose. I’ll be bold enough to break the seal this once.

[He reads.] My thoughts stay with my Silvia every night, and they are slaves to me, who send them flying there. Oh, if their master could come and go as easily, he would lodge himself where they lie, unfeeling. My messenger thoughts rest in your pure bosom, while I, their king, who urges them to go there, curse the good fortune that has blessed them with such favor, because I myself lack my servants’ luck. I curse myself, because I am the one who sends them, so that they rest where their lord should be. What’s this? [He reads.] Silvia, tonight I will set you free. So that’s it. And here’s the ladder for the job. Why, Phaëthon—since you’re a son of Merops like him—will you try to drive the chariot of the sun and burn up the world with your reckless folly? Will you reach for the stars just because they shine on you? Get out, you lowborn intruder, you arrogant slave! Spend your fawning smiles on people of your own rank. And understand that it’s my patience, not anything you deserve, that lets you leave here alive. Thank me for this more than for all the favors I’ve given you, far too many of them. But if you stay in my lands any longer than the fastest possible travel would take you to leave our royal court, then by heaven, my anger will be far greater than any love I ever had for my daughter or for you. Go! I won’t listen to your empty excuses. If you value your life, get away from here fast.
[He exits.]

VALENTINE. And why not death, instead of this living torture? To die is to be banished from myself, and Silvia is my very self. Being banished from her is being cut off from myself—a deadly banishment. What light is light if I can’t see Silvia? What joy is joy if Silvia isn’t near? Unless it’s to imagine that she’s near and feed on the shadow of perfection. Unless I’m with Silvia at night, there’s no music in the nightingale. Unless I can look at Silvia during the day, there’s no day for me to look at. She’s my very being, and I stop existing if I’m not nourished, lit up, cherished and kept alive by her lovely influence. I can’t escape death by fleeing this deadly sentence. If I stay here, I’m just waiting for death. But if I run away from here, I’m running away from life.
[Proteus and Lance enter.]
PROTEUS. Run, boy, run, run, find him.
LANCE. Tally-ho, tally-ho!
PROTEUS. What do you see?
LANCE. The man we’re looking for. There isn’t a hair on his head that isn’t a Valentine.
PROTEUS. Valentine?
VALENTINE. No.
PROTEUS. Who, then? His ghost?
VALENTINE. Neither.
PROTEUS. What, then?
VALENTINE. Nothing.
LANCE. Can nothing talk? Master, should I hit it?
PROTEUS. Who would you hit?
LANCE. Nothing.
PROTEUS. Stop that, you rascal.
LANCE. Why, sir, I’ll hit nothing. Please, let me—
PROTEUS. I said stop it, boy.—Valentine, my friend, a word with you.
VALENTINE. My ears are blocked and can’t hear good news, since they’re already so full of bad.
PROTEUS. Then I’ll bury my news in silence, because it’s harsh, jarring and bad.
VALENTINE. Is Silvia dead?
PROTEUS. No, Valentine.
VALENTINE. Indeed, there’s no Valentine for holy Silvia anymore. Has she broken her promises to me?
PROTEUS. No, Valentine.
VALENTINE. There’s no Valentine at all if Silvia has broken her promises to me. What’s your news?
LANCE. Sir, there’s a proclamation that you’ve been vanished.
PROTEUS. That you’ve been banished—oh, that’s the news—from here, from Silvia and from me, your friend.
VALENTINE. Oh, I’ve already fed on this sorrow, and now too much of it will make me sick. Does Silvia know I’m banished?

PROTEUS. Yes, yes. And to oppose the sentence—which still stands, unreversed and in full force—she offered a sea of melting pearls, which some people call tears. She laid them at her father’s rude feet, and with them her humble self, on her knees. She wrung her hands, whose whiteness suited them so well it was as if they had just turned pale from grief. But neither bent knees, pure hands raised up, sad sighs, deep groans nor silver-flowing tears could get through to her heartless father. Valentine must die if he is caught. Besides that, her pleading made him so angry, when she begged him to call you back, that he ordered her locked up in her room. He made many bitter threats that she would stay there.
VALENTINE. Say no more, unless the next word you speak has some deadly power over my life. If it does, please breathe it into my ear as the final hymn of my endless grief.

PROTEUS. Stop grieving over what you can’t help, and work on finding help for what you’re grieving. Time is the nurse and parent of everything good. If you stay here, you can’t see your love anyway, and staying will also cut your life short. Hope is a lover’s walking stick. Walk away from here with it and use it to fight off thoughts of despair. Your letters can be here even though you’re gone. If you address them to me, I’ll deliver them right into the milk-white bosom of your love. This is no time to argue. Come, I’ll take you through the city gate. Before I leave you, we’ll talk at length about everything to do with your love affairs. For Silvia’s sake, if not your own, take your danger seriously and come with me.
VALENTINE. Lance, please, if you see my boy, tell him to hurry and meet me at the North Gate.
PROTEUS. Go and find him, boy. Come, Valentine.
VALENTINE. Oh, my dear Silvia! Unlucky Valentine!
[Valentine and Proteus exit.]

LANCE. I’m only a fool, you see, and yet I have brains enough to think my master is a kind of a scoundrel. But that doesn’t matter, so long as he’s only one scoundrel. There’s no one alive who knows I’m in love, and yet I am in love. A team of horses won’t drag that secret out of me, or who it is I love. Still, it’s a woman, but what woman I won’t even tell myself. And yet it’s a milkmaid. Yet she’s not a maid, because she’s had godparents for her babies. Yet she is a maid, because she’s her master’s maid and works for wages. She has more skills than a water spaniel, which is a lot for a mere Christian. [He pulls out a paper.] Here’s the cat-alogue of her qualities. First: She can fetch and carry. Why, a horse can’t do more than that. No, a horse can’t fetch, only carry, so she’s better than a nag. Next: She can milk. Look, that’s a sweet virtue in a girl with clean hands.
[Speed enters.]
SPEED. Hello there, Signior Lance! What news with your mastership?
LANCE. With my master’s ship? Why, it’s at sea.
SPEED. Well, the same old bad habit: twisting the words. What news is in your paper, then?
LANCE. The blackest news you ever heard.
SPEED. Why, man? How black?
LANCE. Why, as black as ink.
SPEED. Let me read it.
LANCE. Shame on you, blockhead, you can’t read.
SPEED. You’re lying. I can.
LANCE. I’ll test you. Tell me this: who fathered you?
SPEED. Well, the son of my grandfather.
LANCE. Oh, you illiterate idler! It was the son of your grandmother. This proves you can’t read.
SPEED. Come on, fool, come on. Test me with your paper.
LANCE. [He gives him the paper.] There. And may Saint Nicholas, patron of scholars, help you.
SPEED. First: She can milk.
LANCE. Yes, she certainly can.
SPEED. Next: She brews good ale.
LANCE. And that’s where the saying comes from: “Bless your heart, you brew good ale.”
SPEED. Next: She can sew.
LANCE. That’s the same as asking, “Can she so?”
SPEED. Next: She can knit.
LANCE. Why should a man care about getting a dowry with a girl when she can knit him a stocking?
SPEED. Next: She can wash and scrub.
LANCE. A special virtue, because then she doesn’t need to be washed and scrubbed herself.
SPEED. Next: She can spin.
LANCE. Then I can take life easy, since she can spin for her living.
SPEED. Next: She has many nameless virtues.
LANCE. That’s the same as saying “bastard virtues,” which don’t know who their fathers are and so have no names.
SPEED. Here come her vices.
LANCE. Right on the heels of her virtues.
SPEED. Next: She isn’t to be kissed before breakfast because of her breath.
LANCE. Well, that fault can be fixed with a breakfast. Read on.
SPEED. Next: She has a sweet tooth.
LANCE. That makes up for her sour breath.
SPEED. Next: She talks in her sleep.
LANCE. That doesn’t matter, as long as she doesn’t sleep while she talks.
SPEED. Next: She is slow to speak.
LANCE. Oh, what villain put that down among her vices! Being slow to speak is a woman’s only virtue. Please, cross it out and list it as her chief virtue.
SPEED. Next: She is proud.
LANCE. Cross that out too. It was Eve’s legacy to women and can’t be taken from her.
SPEED. Next: She has no teeth.
LANCE. I don’t care about that either, because I love crusts.
SPEED. Next: She is bad-tempered.
LANCE. Well, the best part is that she has no teeth to bite with.
SPEED. Next: She will often praise her drink.
LANCE. If her drink is good, she may. If she won’t, I will, because good things should be praised.
SPEED. Next: She is too free.

LANCE. She can’t be free with her tongue, because it’s written down that she’s slow to speak. She won’t be free with her purse, because I’ll keep that shut. Now, she may be free with another thing, and I can’t help that. Well, go on.
SPEED. Next: She has more hair than brains, and more faults than hairs, and more money than faults.
LANCE. Stop there. I’ll have her. She was mine and not mine two or three times in that last item. Read it again.
SPEED. Next: She has more hair than brains—

LANCE. More hair than brains. That may be so, and I’ll prove it. The lid of the saltcellar hides the salt, so it’s more than the salt. The hair that covers the brains is more than the brains, because the greater hides the lesser. What’s next?
SPEED. And more faults than hairs.
LANCE. That’s monstrous! Oh, if only that were crossed out!
SPEED. And more money than faults.
LANCE. Why, that word makes the faults attractive. Well, I’ll have her. And if it turns into a match, since nothing is impossible—
SPEED. What then?
LANCE. Why, then I’ll tell you that your master is waiting for you at the North Gate.
SPEED. For me?
LANCE. For you? Yes, who are you? He’s waited for a better man than you.
SPEED. And do I have to go to him?
LANCE. You have to run to him, because you’ve waited so long that walking will hardly do.
SPEED. Why didn’t you tell me sooner? A plague on your love letters!
[He exits.]
LANCE. Now he’ll be beaten for reading my letter. He’s a rude slave who forces his way into secrets. I’ll go after him and enjoy watching the boy get punished.
[He exits.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same. A room in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [The Duke and Thurio enter.]
DUKE. Sir Thurio, don’t worry. She’ll love you now that Valentine has been banished from her sight.
THURIO. Since he was exiled she’s despised me more than ever. She’s sworn off my company and insulted me, so that I’ve given up hope of winning her.

DUKE. This weak impression of love is like a figure carved in ice, which an hour’s heat melts into water so that it loses its shape. A little time will thaw her frozen thoughts, and worthless Valentine will be forgotten.
[Proteus enters.]
Hello, Sir Proteus. Has your countryman left, as our proclamation ordered?
PROTEUS. He’s gone, my good lord.
DUKE. My daughter is taking his departure very hard.
PROTEUS. A little time, my lord, will kill that grief.
DUKE. So I believe, but Thurio doesn’t think so. Proteus, the good opinion I have of you, since you’ve shown some signs of merit, makes me more willing to talk things over with you.
PROTEUS. If I’m ever less than loyal to your Grace, let me not live to look at your Grace again.
DUKE. You know how much I want to arrange the marriage between Sir Thurio and my daughter?
PROTEUS. I do, my lord.
DUKE. And I think you also know how she sets herself against my wishes?
PROTEUS. She did, my lord, when Valentine was here.
DUKE. Yes, and she stubbornly keeps it up. What could we do to make the girl forget her love for Valentine and love Sir Thurio instead?
PROTEUS. The best way is to accuse Valentine of dishonesty, cowardice and low birth, three things women hate deeply.
DUKE. Yes, but she’ll think it’s said out of hatred.
PROTEUS. Yes, if his enemy says it. So it must be said, with convincing details, by someone she thinks of as his friend.
DUKE. Then you must take on the job of slandering him.
PROTEUS. And that, my lord, I’d be reluctant to do. It’s a bad job for a gentleman, especially against his own close friend.
DUKE. Since your praise can’t help him, your slander can’t hurt him either. So the job is neither good nor bad, especially since your friend is the one asking you to do it.

PROTEUS. You’ve convinced me, my lord. If I can manage it by anything I can say to run him down, she won’t go on loving him for long. But even if this uproots her love for Valentine, it doesn’t follow that she’ll love Sir Thurio.

THURIO. So, as you unwind her love from him, you must make sure it doesn’t tangle up and be useful to no one. You need to wind it onto me instead, like thread onto a spool. That must be done by praising me just as much as you run down Sir Valentine.

DUKE. And, Proteus, we can trust you in this matter because we know from Valentine’s account that you’re already a devoted servant of Love and won’t quickly turn traitor and change your mind. On this assurance, you’ll have access to Silvia, where you can talk with her at length. She’s sluggish, heavy-hearted and gloomy, and for your friend’s sake she’ll be glad to see you. There you can work on her with your persuasion to hate young Valentine and love my friend.

PROTEUS. I’ll do as much as I can to make it happen. But you, Sir Thurio, aren’t sharp enough. You have to set traps to catch her desires, the way you smear birdlime on twigs. Use mournful sonnets with carefully crafted rhymes, packed full of vows to serve her.
DUKE. Yes, poetry inspired by heaven has great power.

PROTEUS. Tell her that you’re sacrificing your tears, your sighs and your heart on the altar of her beauty. Write until your ink runs dry, and then wet it again with your tears. Compose some heartfelt line that shows how sincere you are. After all, Orpheus’s lute was strung with the sinews of poets. Its golden touch could soften steel and stone, tame tigers, and make huge sea monsters leave the bottomless depths to dance on the beaches. After you’ve written your sorrowful laments, go at night to your lady’s bedroom window with a sweet band of musicians. Have them play a mournful tune on their instruments. The dead silence of the night will suit that kind of sweet, sad complaint perfectly. This will win her, or nothing will.
DUKE. That kind of training shows you’ve been in love yourself.

THURIO. I’ll put your advice into practice tonight. So, sweet Proteus, my guide, let’s go into the city right away and pick out some gentlemen who are good at music. I have a sonnet that will do the job and get your good advice started.
DUKE. Get to it, gentlemen!
PROTEUS. We’ll stay and attend your Grace until after supper, and then we’ll decide how to proceed.
DUKE. No, get to it right now! I’ll excuse you.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — A forest between Milan and Verona
paragraphs: [Some Outlaws enter.]
FIRST OUTLAW. Hold your ground, men. I see a traveler.
SECOND OUTLAW. Even if there are ten of them, don’t back off. Knock them down.
[Valentine and Speed enter.]
THIRD OUTLAW. Stop, sir, and throw us whatever you’re carrying. If you don’t, we’ll make you sit down and search you.
SPEED. Sir, we’re finished. These are the villains all the travelers are so afraid of.
VALENTINE. My friends—
FIRST OUTLAW. That’s not true, sir. We’re your enemies.
SECOND OUTLAW. Quiet! Let’s hear what he has to say.
THIRD OUTLAW. Yes, by my beard, we will, because he’s a good-looking man.

VALENTINE. Then you should know I have very little money to lose. I’m a man who has been dogged by bad luck. My only riches are these shabby clothes. If you strip me of them here, you take everything I have in the world.
SECOND OUTLAW. Where are you traveling to?
VALENTINE. To Verona.
FIRST OUTLAW. Where have you come from?
VALENTINE. From Milan.
THIRD OUTLAW. Did you stay there long?
VALENTINE. About sixteen months. I might have stayed longer if cruel fortune hadn’t blocked me.
FIRST OUTLAW. What, were you banished from there?
VALENTINE. I was.
SECOND OUTLAW. For what crime?
VALENTINE. For something that pains me to tell you now. I killed a man, and I deeply regret his death. Still, I killed him bravely in a fair fight, without any unfair advantage or low treachery.
FIRST OUTLAW. Well, never regret it if that’s how it was done. But were you really banished for such a small offense?
VALENTINE. I was, and I considered myself lucky to get that sentence.
SECOND OUTLAW. Do you speak foreign languages?
VALENTINE. Traveling when I was young taught me that skill and made me lucky. Otherwise I would often have been miserable.
THIRD OUTLAW. By the bald head of Robin Hood’s fat friar, this fellow would make a fine king for our wild gang.
FIRST OUTLAW. We’ll have him. Men, a word with you.
SPEED. Master, join them. It’s an honorable kind of stealing.
VALENTINE. Quiet, you rascal.
SECOND OUTLAW. Tell us this: do you have anything to live on?
VALENTINE. Nothing but whatever luck brings me.

THIRD OUTLAW. Then you should know that some of us are gentlemen. The wildness of our reckless youth got us thrown out of the company of respectable men. I myself was banished from Verona for plotting to run off with a lady. She was an heiress and a close relative of the Duke.
SECOND OUTLAW. And I was banished from Mantua because of a gentleman I stabbed through the heart in a fit of temper.

FIRST OUTLAW. And I was banished for similar petty crimes. But let’s get to the point. We list our crimes so that they can excuse our lawless lives. And partly we tell you because we see you have a fine figure. By your own account you also speak languages. You’re a man with exactly the kind of accomplishments our profession badly needs—

SECOND OUTLAW. In fact, it’s because you’re a banished man that we’re making this offer to you above anyone else. Would you agree to be our general? Would you make a virtue out of necessity and live the way we do in this wilderness?
THIRD OUTLAW. What do you say? Will you join our band? Say “Yes,” and be captain of all of us. We’ll pay you homage and obey your rule, and love you as our commander and our king.
FIRST OUTLAW. But if you scorn our kind offer, you die.
SECOND OUTLAW. You won’t live to brag about what we offered you.
VALENTINE. I accept your offer and will live with you, on condition that you commit no outrages against helpless women or poor travelers.
THIRD OUTLAW. No, we hate such low, disgusting behavior. Come with us. We’ll take you to our gangs and show you all the treasure we’ve collected. All of it, and all of us, will be at your command.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Milan. The court of the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Proteus enters.]

PROTEUS. I’ve already betrayed Valentine, and now I have to cheat Thurio just as badly. While pretending to speak up for him, I get the chance to push my own love. But Silvia is too beautiful, too faithful, too holy to be corrupted by my worthless gifts. When I swear true devotion to her, she taunts me with how I betrayed my friend. When I dedicate my vows to her beauty, she tells me to remember how I broke my oath by abandoning Julia, whom I loved. She keeps throwing out these sharp remarks, and the smallest of them would crush a lover’s hope. And yet, like a spaniel, the more she kicks my love away, the more it grows and fawns on her. But here comes Thurio. Now we have to go to her window and play some evening music for her.
[Thurio and Musicians enter.]
THURIO. Well now, Sir Proteus, have you crept here ahead of us?
PROTEUS. Yes, gentle Thurio. You know that love will crawl to serve where it can’t walk.
THURIO. Yes, but I hope, sir, that you’re not in love here.
PROTEUS. But I am, sir. Otherwise I wouldn’t be here.
THURIO. With who? Silvia?
PROTEUS. Yes, with Silvia, for your sake.
THURIO. Thank you for that, for your own sake. Now, gentlemen, let’s tune up and play heartily for a while.
[The Host and Julia enter. Julia is dressed in boy’s clothes, disguised as Sebastian.]
HOST. Now, my young guest, I think you’re melancholy. Please tell me, why is that?
JULIA. Well, my host, it’s because I can’t be merry.
HOST. Come on, we’ll cheer you up. I’ll take you somewhere you can hear music and see the gentleman you asked about.
JULIA. But will I hear him speak?
HOST. Yes, you will.
JULIA. That will be music to me.
[Music plays.]
HOST. Listen, listen!
JULIA. Is he one of these men?
HOST. Yes. But quiet, let’s listen to them.
SONG
PROTEUS. Who is Silvia? What is she, that all our young men praise her? She is holy, beautiful and wise. Heaven gave her such grace so that everyone would admire her.
Is she as kind as she is beautiful? Beauty only lives where there is kindness. Love goes to her eyes to cure him of his blindness, and once he can see, he stays and lives there.
So let us sing to Silvia that Silvia is the best of all. She surpasses every mortal thing that lives on this dull earth. Let’s bring her garlands of flowers.
HOST. What’s this, are you sadder than you were before? How are you, man? Don’t you like the music?
JULIA. You’ve got it wrong. It’s the musician who doesn’t like me.
HOST. Why do you say that, my pretty young man?
JULIA. He plays false, old man.
HOST. How, do you mean out of tune on the strings?
JULIA. No, not that. But he’s so false that he hurts the very strings of my heart.
HOST. You have a sharp ear.
JULIA. Yes, and I wish I were deaf. It makes my heart heavy and slow.
HOST. I can see you don’t enjoy music.
JULIA. Not one bit, when it’s this out of tune.
HOST. Listen, what a fine change in the music!
JULIA. Yes, that change is what hurts.
HOST. Would you have them always play just one tune?
JULIA. I would have one man always play just one tune, and be faithful to one woman. But, host, does this Sir Proteus we’re talking about often visit this lady?
HOST. I’ll tell you what Lance, his servant, told me. He loved her beyond all measure.
JULIA. Where is Lance?
HOST. He’s gone to look for his dog. His master has ordered him to take it tomorrow to his lady as a present.
JULIA. Quiet, step aside. The group is breaking up.
PROTEUS. Don’t worry, Sir Thurio. I’ll plead your case so well that you’ll say my clever scheme is the best.
THURIO. Where shall we meet?
PROTEUS. At Saint Gregory’s well.
THURIO. Goodbye.
[Thurio and the Musicians exit.]
