[Silvia appears at the window above.]
PROTEUS. Good evening to your ladyship, madam.
SILVIA. Thank you for your music, gentlemen. Who was that speaking?
PROTEUS. Lady, it’s someone you would quickly learn to recognize by his voice, if you knew how true and pure his heart is.
SILVIA. Sir Proteus, I believe.
PROTEUS. Sir Proteus, gentle lady, and your servant.
SILVIA. What do you want?
PROTEUS. To get what you want, and to win your will.

SILVIA. You have your wish. What I want is this: that you hurry home to bed right now. You sly, lying, false, disloyal man! Do you think I’m so shallow and so stupid that I’d be seduced by your flattery? You’ve already deceived so many with your vows. Go back, go back, and make amends to the woman you loved. As for me, I swear by the pale moon, queen of the night, that I’m nowhere near granting your request. In fact, I despise you for pursuing me so wrongfully. Soon I’ll be scolding myself even for the time I’m wasting talking to you now.
PROTEUS. I admit, sweet love, that I did love a lady. But she’s dead.
JULIA. [Aside.] It would be a lie if I said that, because I know for sure she isn’t buried.
SILVIA. Suppose she is dead. Your friend Valentine is still alive, and as you yourself witnessed, I’m engaged to him. Aren’t you ashamed to wrong him by pestering me like this?
PROTEUS. I’ve also heard that Valentine is dead.
SILVIA. Then suppose I am too, because you can be sure my love is buried in his grave.
PROTEUS. Sweet lady, let me dig it up out of the earth.
SILVIA. Go to your lady’s grave and call her love out of it. Or at least bury your own love in her grave.
JULIA. [Aside.] He didn’t hear that.

PROTEUS. Madam, if your heart is that hard, at least give me your picture to love. I mean the portrait that hangs in your bedroom. I’ll speak to it, sigh over it and weep. Since the real substance of your perfect self is devoted to someone else, I’m nothing but a shadow. So I’ll give my true love to your shadow.
JULIA. [Aside.] If it were a real woman, you’d surely deceive her and turn her into a mere shadow, the way I am now.

SILVIA. I really don’t want to be your idol, sir. But since it suits a liar like you to worship shadows and adore false images, send someone to me in the morning, and I’ll send it to you. And so, good night.
[She exits.]
PROTEUS. It will be as good a night as wretched prisoners have when they wait to be executed in the morning.
[He exits.]
JULIA. Host, shall we go?
HOST. By my holy relics, I was fast asleep.
JULIA. Please tell me, where is Sir Proteus staying?
HOST. Why, at my inn. Believe me, I think it’s almost morning.
JULIA. No, not yet. But this has been the longest night I’ve ever stayed awake through, and the saddest.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The same
paragraphs: [Eglamour enters.]
EGLAMOUR. This is the time when Madam Silvia asked me to come and find out what she wants. There’s some important business she wants me to do for her. Madam, madam!
[Silvia appears at the window above.]
SILVIA. Who’s calling?
EGLAMOUR. Your servant and your friend. Someone who is waiting for your ladyship’s orders.
SILVIA. Sir Eglamour, good morning a thousand times over.
EGLAMOUR. And just as many to you, worthy lady. As your ladyship requested, I’ve come this early to find out what service you’d like me to do for you.

SILVIA. Oh Eglamour, you are a gentleman. Don’t think I’m flattering you, because I swear I’m not. You’re brave, wise, compassionate and highly accomplished. You know very well how much I love the banished Valentine. You also know how my father wants to force me to marry foolish Thurio, whom I hate with my whole soul. You’ve been in love yourself. I’ve heard you say that no grief ever cut so close to your heart as when your lady, your true love, died. You vowed to stay chaste forever over her grave. Sir Eglamour, I want to go to Valentine in Mantua, where I hear he’s living. Since the roads are dangerous to travel, I would like your worthy company. I trust completely in your loyalty and honor. Don’t remind me of my father’s anger, Eglamour. Think instead about my grief, a lady’s grief. Think about how right it is for me to run away to escape a most unholy marriage. Heaven and fortune always punish such marriages with disasters. I beg you, from a heart as full of sorrows as the sea is of sand, to keep me company and go with me. If you won’t, then keep secret what I’ve told you, so that I can risk leaving alone.

EGLAMOUR. Madam, I feel deeply for your troubles. Since I know your feelings are virtuous, I agree to go with you. I care as little about what happens to me as I care much about wishing you every good fortune. When will you leave?
SILVIA. This coming evening.
EGLAMOUR. Where shall I meet you?
SILVIA. At Friar Patrick’s cell, where I plan to go to holy confession.
EGLAMOUR. I won’t let your ladyship down. Good morning, gentle lady.
SILVIA. Good morning, kind Sir Eglamour.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — The same
paragraphs: [Lance enters with his dog, Crab.]

LANCE. When a man’s servant behaves like a cur toward him, you see, it’s hard to take. This is a dog I raised from a puppy. I saved him from drowning when three or four of his blind brothers and sisters went under. I trained him exactly the way someone would say, “This is how I’d teach a dog.” I was sent to give him to Mistress Silvia as a present from my master. I’d barely stepped into the dining room when he trots up to her plate and steals her chicken leg. Oh, it’s an awful thing when a dog can’t behave himself in company! I’d like to have a dog that really takes on the job of being a dog, a dog that’s good at everything, so to speak. If I hadn’t had more brains than him and taken the blame for what he did, I truly think he’d have been hanged for it. As sure as I’m alive, he’d have paid for it. You be the judge. He shoves his way into the company of three or four gentlemanly dogs under the Duke’s table. He hadn’t been there—pardon the expression!—for as long as it takes to piss before the whole room could smell him. “Throw out the dog!” says one. “What mutt is that?” says another. “Whip him out,” says the third. “Hang him,” says the Duke. I’d smelled that smell before, so I knew it was Crab, and I go up to the fellow whose job is whipping the dogs. “Friend,” I said, “are you going to whip the dog?” “Yes, I certainly am,” he said. “Then you’re doing him even more wrong,” I said. “It was me who did the thing you know about.” Without any more fuss he whips me out of the room. How many masters would do that for their servant? No, I swear I’ve sat in the stocks for sausages he’s stolen, or else he’d have been executed. I’ve stood in the pillory for geese he’s killed, or else he’d have paid for it. [To Crab.] You don’t think about any of this now. No, and I remember the trick you played on me when I said goodbye to Madam Silvia. Didn’t I tell you to always watch me and do what I do? When did you ever see me lift my leg and pee against a lady’s hooped skirt? Did you ever see me do a trick like that?
[Proteus enters with Julia, who is disguised as Sebastian.]
PROTEUS. Your name is Sebastian? I like you very much, and I’ll have a job for you shortly.
JULIA. Whatever you like. I’ll do what I can.
PROTEUS. I hope you will. [To Lance.] Well now, you bastard peasant, where have you been loafing around these last two days?
LANCE. Well, sir, I took Mistress Silvia the dog, like you told me to.
PROTEUS. And what does she say about my little jewel?
LANCE. Well, she says your dog was a mutt, and that a mutt’s thanks is good enough for a present like that.
PROTEUS. But she accepted my dog?
LANCE. No, she certainly didn’t. I’ve brought him back here with me.
PROTEUS. What, did you offer her this dog from me?

LANCE. Yes, sir. The other little squirrel of a dog was stolen from me by the hangman’s boys in the marketplace. So then I offered her my own, which is a dog ten times as big as yours, and so the gift was all the greater.
PROTEUS. Go, get out of here and find my dog again, or never come back into my sight. Go away, I said. Are you hanging around here to annoy me? You’re a slave who keeps on bringing me shame.
[Lance exits with Crab.]

Sebastian, I’ve taken you into my service partly because I need a young man like you who can handle my business with some discretion. That stupid oaf over there can’t be trusted. But mostly I hired you for your face and your manners. Unless my instinct is wrong, they show a good upbringing, good fortune and honesty. So understand that this is why I’m taking you on. Go now and take this ring with you. Deliver it to Madam Silvia. The woman who gave it to me loved me very much.
JULIA. It seems you didn’t love her, if you could part with her keepsake. She’s dead, perhaps?
PROTEUS. No, I think she’s alive.
JULIA. Alas!
PROTEUS. Why do you cry “Alas”?
JULIA. I can’t help pitying her.
PROTEUS. Why should you pity her?

JULIA. Because I think she loved you as much as you love your lady Silvia. She dreams of a man who has forgotten her love; you dote on a woman who doesn’t care for your love. It’s a pity love should be so contrary. Thinking about it makes me cry “Alas.”

PROTEUS. Well, give her that ring, and this letter along with it. That’s her room. Tell my lady I’m claiming her promise of her heavenly portrait. When your errand is done, hurry home to my room. You’ll find me there, sad and alone.
[He exits.]

JULIA. How many women would carry a message like this? Alas, poor Proteus, you’ve hired a fox to guard your lambs. Alas, poor fool, why do I pity him when he despises me with all his heart? He despises me because he loves her; I must pity him because I love him. I gave him this ring when he left me, to bind him to remember my love. And now I’m the unhappy messenger. I have to plead for what I don’t want granted, deliver what I’d want refused, and praise his faithfulness, which I’d rather condemn. I’m my master’s true and pledged love, but I can’t be a true servant to my master without being a traitor to myself. Still, I’ll woo for him, but so coldly that, heaven knows, I won’t want him to succeed.
[Silvia enters with her attendants.]
Good day, lady. Please help me find a way to speak with Madam Silvia.
SILVIA. What would you want with her, if I were she?
JULIA. If you are she, I beg you to be patient and hear the message I’ve been sent with.
SILVIA. From whom?
JULIA. From my master, Sir Proteus, madam.
SILVIA. Oh, he’s sent you for a picture?
JULIA. Yes, madam.
SILVIA. Ursula, bring my portrait here.
[The picture is brought to her.]
Go, give your master this. Tell him from me that a certain Julia, whom his fickle thoughts have forgotten, would suit his room better than this shadow of me.
JULIA. Madam, please read this letter.
[She gives her a letter.]
Excuse me, madam, I carelessly handed you a paper I shouldn’t have. This is the letter for your ladyship.
[She takes back the letter and gives her another.]
SILVIA. Please, let me look at that first one again.
JULIA. I can’t, madam. Please forgive me.
SILVIA. There, take it. I won’t look at your master’s lines. I know they’re stuffed with declarations and brand-new oaths. He’ll break them as easily as I tear up his paper.
[She tears the second letter.]
JULIA. Madam, he sends your ladyship this ring.

SILVIA. All the more shame on him for sending it to me. I’ve heard him say a thousand times that his Julia gave it to him when he left. His false finger may have defiled the ring, but mine won’t do his Julia that much wrong.
JULIA. She thanks you.
SILVIA. What did you say?
JULIA. I thank you, madam, for caring about her. Poor lady, my master wrongs her terribly.
SILVIA. Do you know her?
JULIA. Almost as well as I know myself. I swear I’ve wept a hundred separate times just thinking about her troubles.
SILVIA. I suppose she thinks Proteus has abandoned her?
JULIA. I think she does, and that’s the cause of her sorrow.
SILVIA. Isn’t she extremely beautiful?

JULIA. She used to be more beautiful than she is now, madam. When she thought my master loved her dearly, she was, in my judgment, as beautiful as you. But since she stopped bothering with her mirror and threw away the mask that kept off the sun, the weather has withered the roses in her cheeks and nipped the lily-white color of her face. Now she’s become as dark as I am.
SILVIA. How tall was she?

JULIA. About my height. At Pentecost, when all our festival plays were performed, the young men made me play the woman’s part. I was dressed in Madam Julia’s gown, and everyone agreed it fit me as well as if it had been made for me. That’s how I know she’s about my height. And that time I made her cry hard, because I played a tragic part. Madam, it was Ariadne, grieving over Theseus’ broken vows and his cruel desertion. I acted it so vividly, with real tears, that my poor mistress was moved by it and wept bitterly. I wish I may die if I didn’t feel her very sorrow in my heart.

SILVIA. She owes you thanks, kind youth. Alas, poor lady, abandoned and alone! It makes me cry myself to think about what you’ve said. Here, young man, here’s my purse. I give you this for your sweet mistress’ sake, because you love her. Goodbye.
JULIA. And she’ll thank you for it, if you ever meet her.
[Silvia and her attendants exit.]

A virtuous lady, gentle and beautiful. I hope my master’s wooing gets a cold reception, since she cares so much for my mistress’ love. Alas, how love plays games with itself! Here’s her picture; let me look. I think if I had a headdress like that, this face of mine would be every bit as lovely as hers. And yet the painter flattered her a little, unless I’m flattering myself too much. Her hair is auburn; mine is pure golden yellow. If that’s the only difference to his love, I’ll get myself a wig of that color. Her eyes are gray as glass, and so are mine. Yes, but her forehead is low, and mine is high. What could he value in her that I couldn’t make valuable in myself, if this foolish Love weren’t a blind god? Come, shadow, come, pick up this picture, because it’s your rival. Oh, you senseless image, you’ll be worshipped, kissed, loved and adored! If there were any sense in his idol-worship, the real me would be the statue in your place. I’ll treat you kindly for your mistress’ sake, because she treated me kindly. Otherwise, I swear by Jove, I would have scratched out your unseeing eyes to make my master fall out of love with you.
[She exits.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Milan. An abbey
paragraphs: [Eglamour enters.]

EGLAMOUR. The sun is starting to gild the western sky. Now it’s just about the hour when Silvia is supposed to meet me at Friar Patrick’s cell. She won’t fail me, because lovers don’t miss appointments. If anything, they arrive early, they’re in such a hurry.
[Silvia enters.]
Look, here she comes. Lady, a happy evening to you!
SILVIA. Amen, amen. Lead on, good Eglamour, out through the back gate by the abbey wall. I’m afraid I’m being followed by spies.
EGLAMOUR. Don’t be afraid. The forest is less than nine miles away. If we reach it, we’ll be safe enough.
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The same. A room in the Duke’s palace
paragraphs: [Thurio, Proteus and Julia enter.]
THURIO. Sir Proteus, what does Silvia say to my courtship?
PROTEUS. Oh, sir, I find her gentler than she was. But she still objects to your looks.
THURIO. What? That my leg is too long?
PROTEUS. No, that it’s too skinny.
THURIO. I’ll wear a boot to make it look a bit rounder.
JULIA. [Aside.] But love can’t be spurred toward what it hates.
THURIO. What does she say about my face?
PROTEUS. She says it’s a fair one.
THURIO. No, then the flirt is lying; my face is dark.
PROTEUS. But pearls are fair, and as the old saying goes, “Dark men are pearls in beautiful ladies’ eyes.”
JULIA. [Aside.] It’s true, they’re like the pearls, the cataracts, that blind ladies’ eyes. I’d rather shut my eyes than look at them.
THURIO. How does she like my conversation?
PROTEUS. Badly, when you talk about war.
THURIO. But she likes it when I talk about love and peace?
JULIA. [Aside.] She likes it better, actually, when you hold your peace.
THURIO. What does she say about my courage?
PROTEUS. Oh, sir, she has no doubts about that.
JULIA. [Aside.] She doesn’t need to, since she knows it’s cowardice.
THURIO. What does she say about my family?
PROTEUS. That you’re well descended.
JULIA. [Aside.] True, descended from a gentleman down to a fool.
THURIO. Does she think about my property?
PROTEUS. Oh, yes, and she pities it.
THURIO. Why?
JULIA. [Aside.] Because such an ass owns it.
PROTEUS. Because it’s all leased out.
JULIA. Here comes the Duke.
[The Duke enters.]
DUKE. Well now, Sir Proteus! Well now, Thurio! Which of you has seen Sir Eglamour lately?
THURIO. Not me.
PROTEUS. Nor me.
DUKE. Have you seen my daughter?
PROTEUS. No, neither of them.

DUKE. Then she’s run off to that peasant Valentine, and Eglamour is with her. It’s true. Friar Lawrence met them both while he was wandering through the forest doing penance. He knew Eglamour well, and he guessed the other was her. But she was masked, so he couldn’t be sure. Besides, she meant to go to confession at Patrick’s cell this evening, and she wasn’t there. These signs confirm that she’s fled from here. So please, don’t stand around talking. Get on your horses at once and meet me on the rising ground at the foot of the mountain, on the road to Mantua. That’s where they’ve fled. Hurry, dear gentlemen, and follow me.
[He exits.]
THURIO. Well, this is what comes of being a stubborn girl who runs from her good fortune when it chases her. I’ll go after them, more to get revenge on Eglamour than for love of reckless Silvia.
[He exits.]
PROTEUS. And I’ll follow, more for love of Silvia than for hatred of Eglamour, who’s gone with her.
[He exits.]
JULIA. And I’ll follow, more to block that love than from hatred of Silvia, who’s run off for love.
[She exits.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Frontiers of Mantua. The forest
paragraphs: [Silvia and the Outlaws enter.]
FIRST OUTLAW. Come on, come on, be patient. We have to take you to our captain.
SILVIA. A thousand misfortunes besides this one have taught me how to bear this patiently.
SECOND OUTLAW. Come on, bring her along.
FIRST OUTLAW. Where’s the gentleman who was with her?

SECOND OUTLAW. He was quick on his feet and outran us. But Moyses and Valerius are chasing him. You take her to the west end of the wood. Our captain is there. We’ll go after the one who ran. The thicket is surrounded; he can’t escape.
[The Second and Third Outlaws exit.]
FIRST OUTLAW. Come, I have to take you to our captain’s cave. Don’t be afraid. He has an honorable mind and won’t treat a woman lawlessly.
SILVIA. Oh, Valentine, I’m enduring this for you!
[They exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — Another part of the forest
paragraphs: [Valentine enters.]

VALENTINE. How custom breeds habit in a man! I put up with this shady wilderness and these lonely woods better than busy, crowded towns. Here I can sit alone, seen by no one. I can tune my troubles to the nightingale’s mournful song and sing out my sorrows. Oh, you who live in my heart, don’t leave the house empty so long. Otherwise it will fall into ruin, collapse and leave no memory of what it once was. Restore me with your presence, Silvia. You gentle nymph, comfort your forsaken lover.
[Shouts offstage.]

What’s all this shouting and commotion today? It’s my companions, who make their own wishes their law. They’re chasing some unlucky traveler. They’re fond of me, but I have a hard time keeping them from savage violence. Step aside, Valentine. Who’s this coming?
[He steps aside.]
[Proteus, Silvia and Julia, disguised as Sebastian, enter.]

PROTEUS. Madam, I’ve done you this service—though you don’t value anything your servant does—I risked my life and rescued you from the man who would have raped you and forced you to love him. As my reward, grant me just one kind look. I can’t beg a smaller favor than this. And I’m sure you can’t give less than this.
VALENTINE. [Aside.] How like a dream this is, what I’m seeing and hearing! Love, give me patience to hold back for a while.
SILVIA. Oh, how miserable and unhappy I am!
PROTEUS. You were unhappy, madam, before I came. But by coming I’ve made you happy.
SILVIA. By coming near me you make me utterly unhappy.
JULIA. [Aside.] And me too, when he comes near you.

SILVIA. If I’d been caught by a hungry lion, I’d rather have been the beast’s breakfast than be rescued by false Proteus. Oh, heaven, judge how much I love Valentine, whose life is as precious to me as my soul! And just as much—since there can’t be more—I hate false, oath-breaking Proteus. So go away, and don’t pester me anymore.
PROTEUS. What dangerous deed, even one right next to death, wouldn’t I undertake for one gentle look! Oh, it’s the curse of love, and always proven true, that women can’t love where they’re loved.

SILVIA. That Proteus can’t love where he’s loved, you mean. Read Julia’s heart, your first and best love. For her dear sake you once tore your faith into a thousand oaths. And all those oaths sank into perjury when you started loving me. You have no faith left now, unless you have two, and that’s far worse than none. Better to have none than a double faith, which is one too many. You fake, false to your true friend!
PROTEUS. In love, who cares about a friend?
SILVIA. All men except Proteus.
PROTEUS. No, if the gentle power of persuasive words can’t make you any softer, I’ll woo you like a soldier, at sword’s point. I’ll love you against the nature of love—I’ll force you.
[He seizes her.]
SILVIA. Oh, heaven!
PROTEUS. I’ll force you to give in to my desire.
VALENTINE. [He comes forward.] Thug, take your rough, savage hands off her, you rotten excuse for a friend!
PROTEUS. Valentine!

VALENTINE. You ordinary friend, without loyalty or love, which is what friends are like nowadays! Treacherous man, you’ve betrayed my hopes. Nothing but my own eyes could have convinced me. Now I don’t dare say I have a single friend alive; you’d prove me wrong. Who can be trusted, when your own right hand betrays your heart? Proteus, I’m sorry that I can never trust you again. Because of you I must treat the whole world as a stranger. The private wound cuts deepest. Oh, most cursed time, that of all enemies a friend should be the worst!
PROTEUS. My shame and guilt overwhelm me. Forgive me, Valentine. If heartfelt sorrow is enough ransom for an offense, I offer it here. I suffer now as truly as I ever sinned.

VALENTINE. Then I’m repaid, and I accept you as honest once again. Whoever isn’t satisfied by repentance belongs neither to heaven nor earth, because both are satisfied by it. Penitence calms the wrath of the Eternal. And so that my love may appear open and generous, I give you all my claim to Silvia.
JULIA. Oh, poor me!
[She faints.]
PROTEUS. Look after the boy.
VALENTINE. Hey, boy! Hey, lad! What’s wrong? What’s the matter? Look up; speak.
JULIA. Oh, good sir, my master ordered me to deliver a ring to Madam Silvia, and through my carelessness it was never done.
PROTEUS. Where’s that ring, boy?
JULIA. Here it is; this is it.
[She gives him a ring.]
PROTEUS. What? Let me see. Why, this is the ring I gave to Julia.
JULIA. Oh, I beg your pardon, sir, I made a mistake. This is the ring you sent to Silvia.
[She shows another ring.]
PROTEUS. But how did you get this ring? When I left, I gave it to Julia.
JULIA. And Julia herself gave it to me, and Julia herself has brought it here.
[She reveals herself.]
PROTEUS. What? Julia?

JULIA. Look at the woman who was the target of all your oaths and took them deep into her heart. How often you split that heart to the root with your lies! Oh, Proteus, let these clothes make you blush. Be ashamed that I’ve put on such immodest clothing, if there can be shame in a disguise worn for love. Modesty judges it the smaller fault for women to change their outward shape than for men to change their minds.

PROTEUS. Than for men to change their minds! It’s true. Oh, heaven, if man were only constant, he would be perfect. That one flaw fills him with faults and drives him through every sin. Inconstancy gives up before it even begins. What is there in Silvia’s face that I couldn’t see, fresher still, in Julia’s, if I looked with a faithful eye?
VALENTINE. Come, come, give me a hand from each of you. Let me have the blessing of making this happy ending. It would be a pity for two such friends to stay enemies long.
PROTEUS. Heaven be my witness, I have my wish forever.
JULIA. And I have mine.
[The Outlaws enter with the Duke and Thurio.]
OUTLAWS. A catch, a catch, a catch!
VALENTINE. Stop, stop, I tell you! It’s my lord the Duke. Your Grace is welcome to a disgraced man, the banished Valentine.
DUKE. Sir Valentine!
THURIO. There’s Silvia, and Silvia is mine.

VALENTINE. Thurio, back off, or else embrace your death. Don’t come within reach of my anger. Don’t call Silvia yours. If you do it once more, Verona will never see you again. Here she stands. Just try to claim her with a single touch—I dare you even to breathe on my love.
THURIO. Sir Valentine, I don’t care about her, not me. I think a man is a fool to risk his body for a girl who doesn’t love him. I make no claim to her, so she’s yours.

DUKE. All the more degenerate and low you are, to go to such lengths to win her and then drop her on such flimsy terms. Now, by the honor of my ancestors, I applaud your spirit, Valentine, and I think you worthy of an empress’ love. So know this: I now forget all past grievances, cancel all grudges and call you home again. I declare a new standing for you, based on your unrivaled merit, and I sign my name to it like this: Sir Valentine, you are a gentleman, and of good birth. Take your Silvia, because you have earned her.
VALENTINE. Thank you, your Grace; that gift has made me happy. Now I beg you, for your daughter’s sake, to grant me one favor I’m going to ask of you.
DUKE. I grant it for your own sake, whatever it is.

VALENTINE. These banished men I’ve been living with are men gifted with worthy qualities. Forgive them for what they’ve done here, and let them be called back from exile. They’ve reformed; they’re civil and full of good, and fit for important work, my worthy lord.
DUKE. You’ve won; I pardon them and you. Place them as you think their merits deserve. Come, let’s go; we’ll end all our quarrels with celebrations, laughter and splendid ceremony.
VALENTINE. And as we walk along, I’ll be bold enough to make your Grace smile with our conversation. What do you think of this page boy, my lord?
DUKE. I think the boy has grace in him; he’s blushing.
VALENTINE. I promise you, my lord, there’s more grace in him than boy.
DUKE. What do you mean by that?

VALENTINE. If you like, I’ll tell you as we go along, and you’ll be amazed at what has happened. Come, Proteus, your only punishment is to hear the story of your love affairs revealed. After that, our wedding day will be yours too: one feast, one house, one shared happiness.
[They exit.]
